questions.q: What governance surface does the lesson say generative AI adds that a predictive model with fixed inputs/outputs doesn't have?
options: The prompt and the generated output themselves, since a user can type anything and the model can generate almost anything back
The need for a GPU instead of a CPU
A requirement to use only structured numeric inputs
The elimination of any need for access control
questions.explain: The lesson's core distinction is that generative models accept open-ended input and produce open-ended output, which a fixed-schema classifier never has to govern.

questions.q: What is 'prompt injection,' as defined in the lesson?
options: Input, direct or embedded in content the model reads, designed to override the system's intended instructions
A technique for speeding up model training
A method for compressing a model's weights
The standard process of writing a system prompt during development
questions.explain: Prompt injection is specifically about overriding intended behavior through crafted input, not a normal development or optimization technique.

options: A confident, fluent model output that isn't actually supported by any real, verifiable source
A model crashing and producing no output at all
A deliberate test conducted by the security team
An output that is always obviously and visibly wrong
questions.explain: The lesson specifically notes hallucinated output is dangerous because it looks just as authoritative as a correct answer — not because it's obviously wrong.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say human review sampling plays a bigger role for generative models than for a typical classifier?
options: A classifier's output is a score that's easy to monitor statistically, while a generative model's free-text output can be wrong in ways a dashboard metric won't catch
Classifiers never require any monitoring at all
Human reviewers are faster than automated systems at every task
Generative models cannot be monitored with any automated tooling
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts an easily-monitored numeric score against free text that can be subtly wrong, which is why sampling-based human review becomes standard practice.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what four questions does a prompt/output governance policy need to answer, regardless of vendor?
options: Can instructions be overridden, is sensitive info blocked from output, are unverifiable claims flagged, and how long are prompts retained and reviewed
What color scheme the chatbot uses, and its response speed
Only the model's training cost in dollars
Whether the model was trained using cloud or on-premises hardware
questions.explain: These four categories — override resistance, PII handling, factual-claim verification, and retention/review — are the ones the lesson lists as what a real policy must cover.
